Being emotionally close or intimate with others

issues.item: Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma, 'comments on family' is not impossible as a trigger, but paired with the rest of the profile it lacks a clear assault-linked context. The other triggers and memory items point to sensory/intrusive re-experiencing, whereas this item suggests a family-related theme not represented elsewhere in threat, appraisals, or memory.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: 'Avoid grief reminders' implies a bereavement/loss-focused coping target, but no other selected items indicate death loss or grief as a central aspect of the assault trauma. This maladaptive strategy does not fit the rest of the profile, which centers on assault-related intrusive memory, dissociation, and social avoidance.

vignette:
David is a 68-year-old married school counselor who came to treatment after months of telling himself that, at his age, he should have been able to put the assault behind him. Before it happened, he had spent years being the steady person in other people’s crises, the one students sought out when they were overwhelmed or ashamed. The assault occurred after an evening school function when he stopped on his way home. He was attacked by another man at close range, and what has stayed with him are not a full sequence of events so much as a set of fixed images: a face suddenly too near his own, the flash of a bottle, the sharp smell of alcohol on the man’s breath, and the sterile sting of antiseptic later when he was treated. He can describe those moments with unnerving clarity, but not as a smooth story. In session he returns to them as if they are photographs: one frame of being grabbed, another of realizing he could smell liquor, another of lying under bright lights with disinfectant in the air. Remembering them does not feel like remembering to him. It feels, in his words, “like being put right back there,” with the same terror rising in his chest as if the danger were present again.

In the weeks afterward, David noticed that pieces of the assault began appearing without warning. He might be pouring coffee in the faculty lounge and suddenly have a vivid fragment of the attacker’s face in his mind, only for it to vanish just as quickly. Walking past the nurse’s office at school, the clean medicinal smell would catch him off guard and for a second he would be back under hospital lights. Passing a parent at an evening event and catching the smell of alcohol on someone’s clothes or breath could stop him in place internally, even if outwardly he kept moving. He found these moments especially unsettling because they seemed to come from nowhere and disappear before he could get hold of them, leaving behind a jolt of fear and the sense that he was not fully in the present.

He also became aware that emotional closeness had begun to feel dangerous in a way he could not easily explain to himself or to his wife. When someone moved toward him in a warm, confiding way, part of him braced. In his office at school, students often leaned in and spoke quietly about painful family situations or private fears, and David had once regarded that intimacy as central to his work. Since the assault, those encounters could leave him feeling exposed and cornered. He had come to dread moments when another person’s vulnerability invited his own presence in return. At home, when his wife tried to ask what was happening or sat close beside him in bed, he often pulled away emotionally, telling himself he was tired or not in the mood to talk. What frightened him most was not simply being reminded of the event, but the feeling that closeness itself left him unguarded.

Over time he developed ways of getting through these moments that seemed to help in the instant but steadily narrowed his life. When he felt overwhelmed by a smell, a memory fragment, or another person getting too close, he would deliberately try to leave his body or blank out. He described staring at a fixed point, letting the room go far away, and trying not to feel anything until the moment passed. He also began avoiding people more generally. At school he kept his office door closed more often, shortened appointments when he could, and relied on more procedural conversations with students and staff. His colleagues noticed he was less available and less easy with casual talk, though he brushed this off as fatigue. At home the distance was harder to dismiss. His wife experienced him as absent even when he was sitting beside her, and he knew that was true. He avoided intimacy not because he no longer cared for her, but because caring and being emotionally reached felt perilously close to the helplessness he remembered from the assault.

By the time he sought help, the pattern had become difficult to contain. A recent visit to the hospital for a routine medical appointment had gone badly; the antiseptic smell hit him the moment he entered, and the old terror surged so forcefully that he had to focus on going blank just to stay in the building. Not long after, a student had become tearful in his office, and David felt himself withdrawing even as he knew the boy needed him present. That shook him. He began to fear that the parts of him he valued most—his ability to be with people, to let his wife near him, to remain grounded when someone else was distressed—were slipping out of reach. He came to treatment hoping, cautiously, that he might be able to remember what happened without being hurled back into it, and most of all that closeness with other people would stop feeling like a threat.
